 TCNJ recognized nationally for 2026 nonpartisan student voter turnout efforts 
 Posted on November 18, 2026 
 The College of New Jersey has been named a 2026 ALL IN Most Engaged Campus for College Student Voting, recognizing its outstanding efforts to increase nonpartisan student voter participation and make civic engagement an integral part of the college experience.   
 TCNJ is among 273 colleges and universities across the country recognized by the ALL IN Campus Democracy Challenge. To qualify, schools must demonstrate an ongoing commitment to student democratic engagement by meeting several criteria, including:  
     Ongoing participation in the ALL IN Campus Democracy Challenge 
     Development and submission of a nonpartisan democratic engagement action plan with ALL IN in 2026 
     Having a current signatory to ALL IN’s Higher Education Presidents’ Commitment to Full Student Voter Participation 
     Previous recognition with a 2026 Highly Established Action Plan  
 “We want students to see civic engagement as more than something that just happens during an election year,” said Avani Rana , director of co-curricular leadership development at TCNJ. “It’s about helping them understand the issues that shape their communities and feel empowered to participate in our democracy.” 
 For example, a grant from the ALL IN Campus Democracy Challenge supported initiatives encouraging students to vote early. A Party to the Polls event brought more than 180 students together for food, music from student DJs, conversations about voting plans, and rides to the early voting location.  
 TCNJ Votes fellows — undergraduate students who develop and lead civic engagement programming — also played an important role in expanding the outreach. 
 “Thanks to the work of TCNJ Votes fellows, we were able to engage many different groups on campus,” said graduate student Sarah Kasziba-O’Rahilly , who worked with Rana on TCNJ Votes initiatives. “This year, we focused on engaging our student athletes, Greek life, and cultural organizations through events that encouraged a wider range of students to participate in our events and in elections.”  
 Kasziba-O’Rahilly said the work has been especially rewarding because it creates opportunities for students to ask questions and develop a plan to vote and follow through on Election Day. 
 “Our Most Engaged Campus honorees prove that when institutions invest in nonpartisan campus voter turnout, students will show up at the ballot box in a big way,” said Jen Domagal-Goldman, executive director of the ALL IN Campus Democracy Challenge. 
 “The data doesn’t lie — young voters had a decisive impact on races across the country this year, showing the immediate impact of this work. ALL IN celebrates these colleges and universities for their commitment and for the long-term efforts they have implemented to make civic engagement not just a defining feature of campus life this year, but a long-term habit for students to carry with them for the rest of their lives.”  
 More than 1,065 campuses across all 50 states and Washington, D.C., are part of ALL IN, including more than 275 community colleges and 300 Minority Serving Institutions. These institutions collectively serve nearly 11 million students. 
 —  Emily W. Dodd ’03
